newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters meet Herman, arrests made in Miami.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters meet Herman, arrests made in Miami.

text.p: Talks aimed at ending the 8-day-old strike at United Parcel Service got under way at the Labour Department on Monday amid signs the dispute was becoming violent.
Miami police said they charged three striking UPS drivers with attempted murder in an attack on another UPS driver with an ice pick as he was making deliveries.

Separate meetings between Teamsters union and United Parcel Service officials were being held with Labour Secretary Alexis Herman in a bid to end the strike at the United States' largest package carrier.
Herman requested the meetings after talks between the parties broke down Saturday despite the assistance of a federal mediator.

"I intend to talk with each party individually to find out what it will take to move these talks forward and to urge greater flexibility and a willingness to compromise to get back to the bargaining table," she said in a statement.
UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich spoke to reporters at the Labour Department and repeated the company's call for President Bill Clinton to intervene.
Earlier Monday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the strike was a concern, but that the conditions for federal intervention had not yet been met.

In Nashville, Tenn., a UPS driver was killed when his tractor-trailer toppled off a freeway ramp and fell onto busy Interstate 65. The company said the man was a long-time UPS driver-trainer who was substituting for a regular driver because of the strike.
In Miami, police said Roderick Carter, working in defiance of the strike, was attacked Thursday when his UPS truck stopped at a traffic light.
Angel Mielgo, 30; Orestes Espinosa, 30; and Benigno Rojas, 28, were charged with attempted murder. Adran Paez, 25, was charged with aggravated battery.
"All are UPS workers," police spokeswoman Nina Fonticiella said. "This is the only incident we've had like this, but tension is mounting."
Teamsters spokeswoman Nancy Stella said the union did not have details on the incident but said: "We are urging our locals to refrain from violence."
Labour Secretary Herman had warned Sunday against any move by UPS to hire substitutes for striking workers and urged the two sides to resume talks without escalating the dispute.
"I believe hiring replacement workers does contribute to that escalation," Herman said on the CNN programme "Late Edition."

Executives of Atlanta-based UPS, which before the strike delivered about 80 percent of all packages shipped by ground nationwide, said they wanted to avoid hiring replacement workers but declined to rule out such a move.
"The last thing we want to do, the last thing I want to do, is replace UPS workers," Chief Executive Officer James Kelly, said on the CBS programme "Face the Nation."
But he left open the possibility, saying UPS was losing "hundreds of millions of dollars a week."
UPS normally handles 12 million packages a day. Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells has described the strike as the biggest in the United States in the past 25 years.

Other package carriers have leaped into the gap left by the strike. The U.S. Postal Service said the strike was swelling its business to Christmas-season levels and added rare Sunday deliveries of packages in some places.
UPS' Kelly said Sunday that he saw a role for President Clinton, who could suspend a strike for 30 days if it created a sufficiently large economic emergency.
But White House spokesman McCurry said Monday that the conditions for intervention under the Taft-Hartley law had still not been met.

"The standard in the statute hasn't changed in the last week -- it's 'imperil the national health and safety' -- and we monitor the strike conditions and the economic conditions to see if that standard has been met," McCurry said. "So far it has not."
